# Building a Self-Evolving AI Infrastructure: The OpenCode Evolution

What happens when you give an AI the power to improve its own tooling? Over the past three weeks, I've been running an experiment in self-evolving infrastructure — an AI-powered system that creates its own skills, manages its own knowledge, and progressively simplifies its own complexity. Here's what I've learned.

<img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="System Architecture" style="display:block;width:100%;max-width:900px;height:auto;margin:1.5rem auto;">

## The Three-Week Sprint

This wasn't a planned project. It started with a simple observation: my AGENTS.md file had grown to 1,637 lines of sprawling instructions that no model — including frontier ones — could follow consistently. The system needed radical simplification.

<img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="Evolution Timeline" style="display:block;width:100%;max-width:900px;height:auto;margin:1.5rem auto;">

### Week 1: Foundation (March 21–28)

The first week focused on building the content pipeline. I published the **Life Orchestrator 5-post series**, a deep exploration of personal automation using the Plant → Grow → Harvest → Rest lifecycle model. Each post went through Directus CMS and rendered on Astro 6.0 with interactive diagrams.

Then came the breakthrough: I installed **12 agentsys skills** — consult, deslop, discover-tasks, drift-analysis, and a suite of enhance-* tools. These weren't just utilities; they formed the backbone of a self-improving system.

The week closed with the **Nvidia GTC 2026 blog post**, proving the content pipeline could handle real-time event coverage.

### Week 2: Radical Simplification (March 31–April 3)

This is where things got interesting. I introduced **8 core principles** and the TELOS framework — an AI constitution governing every decision the system makes. The ultimate goal: all instructions, schemas, and workflows should be designed so smaller open-source models (7B-14B) can execute them correctly.

Then came the **Hub & Spoke restructuring**:

> [!NOTE] The Numbers
> - **AGENTS.md**: 1,637 → 293 lines (**5.6x reduction**)
> - **Skill Factory**: 2,910 → 314 lines (**9.2x reduction**)
> - **12 context files** created for progressive disclosure

The principle was simple: one hub file loads only what's needed, when it's needed. No model should have to parse 1,600 lines to find the one instruction it needs.

<img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="Skill Factory Pipeline" style="display:block;width:100%;max-width:900px;height:auto;margin:1.5rem auto;">

### Week 3: Knowledge Engine (April 5–8)

The most recent work introduced the **Brainplane Protocol** — a knowledge engine that captures messy session output, cleans it, and files it into a structured wiki. The agent reads the wiki for context (never the raw dumps), creating a self-improving feedback loop.

<img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="Brainplane Protocol" style="display:block;width:100%;max-width:900px;height:auto;margin:1.5rem auto;">

The wiki now covers:

- **Karpathy Patterns** — LLM knowledge base patterns derived from Andrej Karpathy's coding methodology
- **GLM-5 Agentic Systems** — Production patterns for tool-calling agents
- **Contamination Mitigation** — Preventing knowledge pollution between sessions
- **Omnimemory Architecture** — Persistent memory across conversations
- **Automated Knowledge Compiler** — Converting raw input to structured knowledge

## The Architecture: Why It Works

Three design decisions made everything click:

**1. Progressive Disclosure Everywhere.** Skills, menus, documentation — all structured in layers (L0 minimal → L4 full reference). The system loads only what's needed for the current task. This is why 69 skills don't create cognitive overload.

**2. Schema-First Design.** Every skill follows an identical schema validated by Pydantic. Menus are generated at runtime from configuration files, never hardcoded. This means the system can create and improve its own tools deterministically.

**3. Cost-Aware Model Routing.** Frontier models handle high-cognition tasks (architecture decisions, deep reasoning). Edge models handle routine tasks (single file changes, quick operations). This dual-tier strategy keeps costs sustainable.

<details>
<summary>Technical Deep Dive: The Stack</summary>

| Component | Technology | Port | Purpose |
|-----------|-----------|------|---------|
| Agent Runtime | OpenCode + GLM-5 | — | Primary AI interface |
| CMS | Directus | 8055 | Content management API |
| Blog Engine | Astro 6.0 | 3002 | Static site with interactive components |
| Chat API | FastAPI | 8057 | Streaming chat with GLM-5 |
| Memory | PostgreSQL + pgvector | 5432 | 1,520 memories with semantic search |
| Monitoring | Prometheus + Grafana | 9090/3003 | System observability |
| Containers | Docker | — | 52 running services |
| Knowledge Base | Brainplane Wiki | — | Structured knowledge engine |

The system runs on a single server with 7.5 GiB RAM and 80% disk utilization. Efficiency isn't just a goal — it's a constraint that forces better design.

</details>

## What's Next

The roadmap sits at **81% (9/11 items)**. The remaining items:

- **Schema Infrastructure v2.0** — A composition layer for building complex schemas from simple primitives
- **Skill Publication as Journey Kits** — Packaging skills for distribution to other OpenCode users
- **Domain Setup** — orchestr8.com, schemafactory.com, brainplane.dev

The deferred backlog holds 30+ items, from LLM middleware (Plano) to an email SMTP setup for analytics escalation. Each one is captured, prioritized, and waiting.

## The Meta-Lesson

The most surprising insight? **The system improves faster when you constrain it.** The 5.6x reduction in AGENTS.md didn't remove capability — it focused it. Every byte that a 7B model doesn't have to parse is a byte of context budget saved for actual reasoning.

This is the Karpathy principle applied to infrastructure: the simplest system that solves the problem is the best system. Not because simplicity is inherently good, but because complexity is inherently expensive — especially when your compute budget is measured in tokens.
